name: Trading Psychology
goal: Recognise the biases and emotions that make traders break their rules, and build habits that keep you consistent.
milestones: Write a one-page trading plan and follow it for 20 simulator trades.
Journal every trade with your emotion and one lesson.
Do a weekly review for 4 weeks in a row.

lessons.title: Cognitive biases
body: Loss aversion: losses hurt roughly twice as much as equal gains feel good (Kahneman and Tversky). This makes traders hold losers too long, hoping to get back to break-even, and sell winners too early.
Confirmation bias: we look for information that supports our position and ignore what contradicts it. Fix: before entering, write what would prove you wrong.
Recency bias: the last few trades feel more important than the last hundred. Three losses in a row do not mean your strategy stopped working; a few hundred trades might.
Overconfidence: after a winning streak, traders increase size and break rules. Some of the biggest losses come right after the best weeks.
keyTakeaways: Loss aversion makes us hold losers and cut winners.
Define what proves you wrong before entering.
Judge a strategy on a large sample, not the last few trades.
lessons.exercise: Review your journal: find one trade affected by each bias above.

lessons.title: Fear, greed, FOMO and revenge trading
body: Fear makes you skip valid setups or exit too early. Greed makes you oversize or move your target further away. FOMO (fear of missing out) makes you chase a move that already happened, entering late with a bad stop.
Revenge trading is trying to win back a loss immediately, usually with bigger size and a worse setup. It is the fastest route to a blown account.
Practical defences: a maximum number of trades per day, a daily loss limit after which you stop, a mandatory break after two losses in a row, and fixed position sizing calculated before entry.
Mark Douglas taught thinking in probabilities: any single trade's result is random; only the series matters. When you truly accept that, a loss stops feeling personal.
keyTakeaways: Name the emotion before you act on it.
Hard rules (daily loss limit, max trades) beat willpower.
Each trade is one of the next hundred.
lessons.exercise: Add a rule to your plan: 'After 2 losses in a row I stop for the day.' Follow it in the simulator.

lessons.title: The trading plan
body: A trading plan is a written document that answers: what markets and timeframes I trade; my setups with exact entry, stop and exit rules; my risk per trade, per day and per week; when I trade and when I do not; and how I review.
If a rule cannot be checked as 'followed' or 'not followed', it is not a rule. 'Buy strong stocks' is vague; 'Buy when price closes above the 20-day high while above the 50 SMA' is a rule.
Your plan turns trading from emotional decisions into executing a process. Your goal each day becomes 'follow the plan', not 'make money'.
Review and update the plan monthly, based on journal data, not on feelings after one bad day.
keyTakeaways: Write it down: markets, setups, risk, schedule, review.
lessons.exercise: Use docs/templates/TRADING-PLAN.md to write your first plan.
readMore: Alexander Elder, 'The New Trading for a Living' (record keeping and plan)
Van K. Tharp, 'Trade Your Way to Financial Freedom'

lessons.title: Journaling and review
body: Professional traders keep detailed records: date, instrument, setup, entry, stop, target, exit, size, result in R, screenshot, emotion and lesson. The Trading journal in this app stores the core of this.
Weekly review questions: Did I follow my plan? Which setup made money and which lost? Were my losses caused by the market or by mistakes? What one thing will I improve next week?
Separate good decisions from good outcomes. A trade that followed the plan and lost is a good trade. A trade that broke the rules and won is a bad trade that teaches a dangerous lesson.
Over months, your journal becomes your best data source: it shows which conditions suit your strategy and where you leak money.
lessons.exercise: Run a weekly review using docs/templates/WEEKLY-REVIEW.md.

quiz.prompt: Holding a losing trade hoping it returns to break-even is mostly caused by:
quiz.explanation: Losses hurt more than gains please, so we avoid realising them.

quiz.prompt: You lose three trades in a row with a tested strategy. The best reaction is:
options: Double size to win it back
Follow your plan; check whether the losses broke any rules
Switch to a different market immediately
quiz.explanation: Short losing streaks are normal. Judge on large samples and process.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a good trading rule?
options: Buy on a daily close above the 20-day high if price is above the 50 SMA
quiz.explanation: A rule must be objective and checkable.

quiz.prompt: A trade broke your rules but made money. It was:
options: A bad decision with a lucky outcome
Trying to win back a loss immediately, often with bigger size
quiz.explanation: It is emotional, oversized and usually ends badly.

quiz.prompt: Which defence against emotional trading is the strongest?
options: Hard written rules like a daily loss limit
quiz.explanation: Pre-committed rules work when emotions are high; willpower does not.

options: Chasing moves late with poor stops
quiz.explanation: Fear of missing out makes traders enter after the move, with bad reward-to-risk.
